newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia fights to control AIDS.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia fights to control AIDS.

text.p: The organisers of World Aids Day in Indonesia said on Sunday they saw hope in the fight against the disease but expressed concern that official statistics underestimated the prevalence of the virus.
Martina Widjaya, chairwoman of the Indonesian AIDS Foundation (YAI), said the ninth World AIDS day would remind Indonesians they were at a crucial point in the fight against the HIV virus.

"It is like a wave coming in," Martina said of HIV, the virus that leads to the Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome, or AIDS. HIV kills or impairs cells of the immune system, destroying the body's ability to fight infection.
"Thailand closed its eyes because of the tourism. For us, Indonesia, it is not yet that bad. We can hold the growth of HIV carriers," she said.
Indonesia has an official HIV/AIDS toll of 465 but health workers said these figures only represent reported cases and the real figure could be as much as a hundred times greater.
"Figures come from those detected. Nobody knows how much the real figures are," Mawawati, an official at the Indonesian Health Department, told Reuters on Sunday.
The World Health Organisation (WHO) has said as many as 500,000 may be HIV infected in Indonesia.
Indonesia marked World AIDS day with an official opening in central Jakarta attended by Social Affairs Minster Inten Suweno.

Rock bands, comedians and traditional 'Dangdut' music stars performed in a day-long festival to promote AIDS awareness at Jakarta's Ancol theme park. Student volunteers wearing the red AIDS ribbon handed out condoms to suprised looking passers-by.

However, in a country where talk about condoms is still very much taboo, the fight against AIDS must be based on changing people's sexual behaviour using rubber prophylactics as a last resort, Widjaya said.
"Condoms are a last resort. Our religion does not allow us to talk about condoms. It is not our way of life," she said.
Indonesia, a country of almost 200 million, is 85 percent Moslem and the promotion of condoms has often been criticised by religious leaders as tantamount to promoting promiscuity.

Lubis Firman, a medical doctor and head of Kusuma Buana, a non-governmental organisation (NGO) that promotes AIDS awareness amongst sex workers, said Indonesia needed to be more realisitic about preventative contraception.
"Many studies have proven that Indonesians have multiple sex partners behaviour that gives Indonesia the potential for the rapid spread of AIDS," Firman said.

Widjaya said if Indonesia is to avoid an AIDS explosion it must ask quickly and this means by-passing bureaucratic government procedures and raising money straight from business. YAI is 100 percent private-funded, she said.
"We have to be optimistic. Otherwise why do we do this," Widjaya said. "We can help our next generation."
